newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain's Telefonica shares seen unstoppable.
newsitem.headline: Spain's Telefonica shares seen unstoppable.

text.p: The upward swing of Spanish telecoms operator Telefonica, whose shares hit year-end predictions in May, seems limitless, analysts said on Monday.

"While the upward trajectory of the bourse continues, Telefonica shares will also climb," said an analyst at a Spanish bank who put the short-term mark for Telefonica shares at above 4,500 pesetas after they set a new record at 4,440 earlier.

Telefonica has climbed 45 percent since the start of the year, almost double the rise of the overall market, boosted by both its privatisation in February and its new alliances with Portugal Telecom, and above all, with British Telecommunications and MCI Corp.

Telefonica chairman Juan Villalonga, a firm defender of the notion of "shareholder value", said the BT/MCI deal would convert his company into the fifth largest telecoms operator in the world by capitalisation.
"This promise signifies that Telefonica should be valued at about 6,000 pesetas per share," said the head of variable income trading at a big Spanish bank.
Analysts said there had been little activity at an operating level to justify such big share gains, but the recent share swap deals with PT and BT could be partly responsible for the rise.

"The accords signed with PT and BT foresee that these two operators acquire a total of three percent of the capital of Telefonica, some six million shares, and although they have between six months and a year, the buying could have started," the variable income head said.

Experts said another factor influencing the share price was the increasing clarity surrounding the end of a pact between Telefonica and the joint venture Unisource that had been making dealers nervous.

"The negotiations with Unisource seem to be on good footing and if the press reports are confirmed, Telefonica will not have to pay any compensation (to Unisource)," an analyst from a foreign bank said.
Domestically, the relatively slow process of privatisation of Retevision, Telefonica's future competitor in basic telephone services, was also seen helping push up shares.
"We are about to raise our objective for the price of the shares of Telefonica without have changed our results forecasts," another analyst said.
The analysts were in agreement that there were few factors that could block the upward trajectory of the company, with one commenting that Telefonica was "in a state of free climb".
